title: Matlock and Bob McCracken as accomplished but non-influential clarinetists
summary: Chace sees no Chicago influence from Matlock or McCracken, from whom he bought his first clarinet, calling them competent players without personality.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Who are we talking about on all the West Coast records? The clarinet player who does so much arraignment? Matlock.
Well, Matlock, on the other hand, he was playing for several years in Chicago with the Bobcats, and everybody got to know him. Now, do you feel that he might have left an influence?

Perhaps, but I'm simply not competent to say. It's almost 25 years since that time, isn't it? Yes. And I don't hear any talk about Matlock among different clarinet players. He's, of course, he's now one of the chieftains of the L.A. School of Playing, and everybody admires his work, but in connection with Chicago or the Bobcats, I don't hear anything.

The clarinetist who left Chicago and has joined those West Coast boys. Bob McCracken? McCracken, for one. I don't hear anything particularly derivative in Bob, nor anything particularly characteristic. Am I right about that? I think so.

When I was first learning how to play, I bought a clarinet from McCracken. I was very young, and I asked him what he thought of Pee-wee Russell, and he demurred for a moment, and then he said, well, Pee-wee's a stylist. And then either said nothing or talked about something else. McCracken, I guess, is, as far as I know, an extremely accomplished clarinet player, but my opinion is that there are thousands like that, and it's awfully hard to try to figure out what connection they have with traditional jazz. I don't know where they learned. I guess they learned how to play clarinet, and somebody gave them a Dixieland job, and that's the way they grew up.

They learned the tunes, and they may have shaped the tune a little in terms of what they heard somebody else play, but retained an indifference rather than developed a personality or developed a copy style.

That's a good word, personality, yeah. And there are so many of these guys, they're not interested in individuating themselves or differentiating themselves from other players. Their mark of excellence is a kind of competence. Stay in tune and play fleetly, and then you have it. You're a good musician. I think McCracken came from Texas. Is that right? I believe he did, yes.
He might have passed through some of the southern influences.

That's true, but I haven't heard him very much, and certainly not in recent years. He's in L.A., I believe. But we seem to be talking about McCracken, and he's just one of many guys that I don't think is helpful in trying to discuss tendencies or influences in clarinet playing.
